Hint 2 says 'The length property counts every character', which names the exact property the answer consists of (title.length); hint 1 already says it is a property and not a method. The learner only has to type the name.
Hint 3 says 'The word is false', which states the printed word outright; the learner only has to add the brackets.
Hint 3 says the type has the same name as the value itself; with 'typeof undefined' on screen this states the answer.

Hint 1 says to look at the 'three names' inside the last line, but the line has only two variable names (trail and km); the middle operand is a quoted space. A learner counting names is pointed the wrong way.
The feedback for both wrong options (40 and 50) says that line 2 stops the program with an error or throws one. That names the correct outcome, so the learner has no second attempt left to work out.

The prompt says typed may be text and target is the number to match, which also fits Number(typed) === target. The fifth test passes the text '12' as target, so that reading fails a test the prompt never mentions; only typed == target passes.

Hint 1 says 'Use a ternary', which names the construct the solution is built on. Hint 1 should only point at where to look; the construct belongs to hint 2, so the first hint already gives away the approach.

Hint 3 states the placement of every remaining line (break check before the adding line, print after the closing brace); together with hint 1 it spells out the whole order, so the learner has nothing left to work out.

The reference link is the Array.prototype.indexOf() page. The item is about reading an item by its index (spices[1]), and indexOf is a different method that finds an index from a value, so a learner who follows the link reads about something else. Property accessors or the Array page fits.

Hint 3 says to 'subtract the smallest step'. Among the chips 0, 1 and 2 the smallest is 0, which is wrong (it reads index 4 and prints undefined), so the phrase can point the learner at the wrong chip.

Hint 3 says the brackets go right after prices and the variable that holds the key goes inside them. The prompt already names that variable (item), so this spells out the whole expression prices[item] and leaves nothing to work out.

The feedback for 'remove' and for 'null' says the code is not valid and fails. That is true only in the second blank. In the first blank both are legal key names (jar.remove = 5, jar.null = 5), the program runs and prints {remove: 5} or {null: 5}, so a learner who tried them there sees a wrong output and not a failure, and the feedback contradicts what they saw.

Hint 2 says a default applies only when the property is missing. In JavaScript a default applies whenever the value is undefined, including a property that exists and holds undefined, so the stated rule is wrong for that case.
objects-in-depth.lesson-1: The card says a default fills in a missing property. A default also applies to a property that exists with the value undefined, so 'missing' is an incomplete rule.

Hint 1 says 'line 'return'' and names found, but the learner has no line numbers and the prompt never defines a variable called found. The hints and explanation use the reference solution's name as if it were given.

Hint 2 contrasts a function declaration with 'a const', but the code uses var for closing. A const would throw a ReferenceError, while the real result is a TypeError, so the hint points at a behaviour that does not match the snippet.

Hint 3 refers to 'the function made by up(markup)', but the prompt defines no helper called up; that is the reference solution's name. A learner cannot tell what up is, and the hint already spells out the whole structure.

Feedback for option 3 says a bound function working on a copy would leave jar at 3. But on a copy the second call would still return 5, not 3, so the belief it describes does not lead to the answer 3. The feedback blurs the value of jar.coins with the value of second.

The feedback of both wrong options reveals the correct answer. Option 'B' says finally's console.log 'happens first, so C prints too', and option 'B\nC' says C prints 'before the returned value reaches the outer console.log'. With only three options, either message gives the exact output 'C then B', so the learner's second attempt needs no thinking.

The explanation says 'use a strict comparison with 5'. In JavaScript 'strict comparison' means === / !==, so a learner may think the fix is a different operator. What is meant is the strictly-greater operator > rather than >=.

The handler prints the string 'btned', which is not a word and looks like a find-and-replace leftover. Learners must compare it letter by letter across the three options and may suspect a typo. A plain word such as 'booked' would keep the focus on how many times the handler runs.

The chips are shared by both blanks, but the feedback for finally says it 'runs after the catch' and makes the last line print undefined. That is true only when finally is put in the second blank. In the first blank there is no catch before it, finally does not handle the rejection, and nothing prints at all (the rejection stays unhandled). A learner who chose finally for the first blank is told something that does not describe their program.

The prompt says Return 'item: retry' and 'item: skip' in quotes, while the tests expect the value of failure.item in front (for example 'bread: retry'). A careful learner can read the quoted text literally and return the fixed string 'item: retry', which fails every test. The prompt should say the returned text is the failure's item, then ': retry'.

Hint 3 says 'The callback is the last thing to run.' That states the position of curtain, which is the whole answer: only one option puts curtain last. Hint 3 should narrow the choice without naming the result.

The explanation says the lookup 'follows the chain from s to shelf'. There is no identifier shelf in the code; the class is Shelf and the object holding the value is Shelf.prototype. A learner can look for a variable that does not exist.
Hint 3 says the text is stored 'on kit', but the code has no kit: the class is Kit and the value sits on Kit.prototype. The hint points at an object that does not exist in the snippet.

The explanation says move() runs 'with this set to critter'. The prompt and the task have no object called critter (the parameter is species, the delegating object is the learner's own, called pet in the reference). The sentence names something that does not exist.

The reference link is the Destructuring page, but the bug is an object spread that copies the shared object. A learner who follows the link to read more finds nothing about spread or copying; the Spread syntax page fits the defect.

Feedback of the option 'A Set keeps every value you give it, repeats included' says the size would be 3 'for any list'. A Set that kept everything would have the size of the list it was given (3 only for this list), so the claim is wrong. The feedback also ends by stating the correct rule (NaN counts as a repeat of itself), which gives the answer away.
Hint 3 ('Create things, add the room, then check the room before the fresh object') spells out the whole order of the program, so the learner no longer has to work out the ordering.
Hint 1 ('Line 2 already shows how to share a symbol') is not a pointer to a place but names the answer of the first blank: line 2 contains Symbol.for, so the learner just copies it.

The prompt asks for 'the names never stopped', but the reference keeps a name that was stopped and then started again (start a, stop a, start a gives ['a']), which is 'still running' and not 'never stopped'. A careful reader of 'never stopped' would return [] for that input. Repeated starts of one name and a stop before a start are also left undefined. Say 'names still running at the end' or specify these cases.

proxy-reflect-metaprogramming.lesson-3: The card says Object.defineProperty sets any flag you leave out to false. That holds only when the property is new. When defineProperty redefines an existing property, an omitted flag keeps its current value (for example, defining {value: 2} on an assigned property leaves it writable, enumerable and configurable). A learner reading the card as a general rule will predict wrongly for existing properties. Say 'for a new property'.

The reference link is the 'for statement' page, but the snippet has no loop. The concept is slice and a page offset, so a learner who follows the link to read more finds nothing about the bug (Array.prototype.slice() would fit).

Hint 3 ('Order the pushes: bake, then the cleanup, then the catch') lists the three pushes in order, which is the printed array apart from the literal values, so the learner no longer has to trace the throw and finally.

debugging.lesson-1: 'A loop that stops at n reads one slot too many, and one that stops at n - 1 skips the last item' can be read two ways: the ordinary loop 'i < n' also stops at n and is correct. The card never says that the bug is a loop that runs while i <= n (or i < n - 1), so a learner may take the correct loop for the faulty one.

The prompt asks 'Which split does that?', but the second and third options begin 'Both:' and 'Neither:', which answer a different question (which methods should move) and do not name any split. A learner cannot tell what 'Both' or 'Neither' refers to. Option 2 (one method per class) would also keep the printed text and give each class one reason to change, so it is a defensible split in practice; only its stated rule is wrong. Phrase all three options as splits.
The explanation says 'Soup is missing, so it adds 0; adding pie to cost would price it.' The code has no soup; the missing kind is pie. The explanation contradicts the snippet and the prompt.
Option 3 says the program throws 'because rates has no pie key', but the table in the code is named cost; there is no rates. The wrong name makes the option read as being about different code.

Option 1 ('off() empties the whole Set, so no listener is left for the second send') is true for this program: show is the only listener, so after off() the Set really is empty and the second send prints nothing. A careful learner can defend it as an observation. Only its implied mechanism (delete clears everything) is wrong, and the feedback ('Any other listener would still be called') talks about a case the snippet does not contain. Add a second listener to the code so the options separate.

The reference link is 'Spread syntax (...)', but the snippet uses no spread and the concept is composition from passed-in functions. A learner who follows the link to read more finds an unrelated page.

The prompt says 'Return new for the first request of each key and same for every later request', but never says what is returned overall. The tests expect an array with one 'new' or 'same' per key, in request order. A learner could return a single string, a count or an object. State that the function returns an array of answers, one per key, in order.

This is the first lesson of the first unit, yet the snippet needs variable declaration with let and reassignment (tray = tray / 4), which the next unit (Variables) teaches. The unit declares no prerequisite for it, and the same applies to the other TRACE items of this unit.

Lesson 3 (predict-01, fill-01, parsons-01 and concept-01) tests how Boolean() converts 0, '0', 'false' and '' to true or false. That is the truthy and falsy rule, which unit 3 (Operators and comparisons, concept truthy-and-falsy) teaches and tests again with Boolean('') and Boolean(' '). The boolean-values concept itself (true and false as values) is only tested by predict-02 and trace-01.

Rated 2, but the learner must write a three-way expression that chains two && checks with ||, relying on && and || returning an operand and on && binding tighter than ||, and must order the checks and choose >= over >. That is more ideas than any other beginner write item, and the learner has not met the ternary yet (lesson 3). It is a 3 for the beginner track.

The line '  if (n === 4) break;' is an if without braces. Every if in the Conditionals unit uses a braced block, so the one-line form was never taught. It also hides the block structure the learner has to arrange, in the lesson's busiest Parsons (six lines, loop, accumulator and break order together).

Rated 2, but the learner must simulate a four-pass loop with continue for each value of skip and then spot the closed form 10 - skip; no code about break or continue is written. Deriving a formula from a described loop is more than one idea at once and is a 3 for the beginner track.

The reference points to Array.prototype.indexOf(), which finds the index of a value. The item is about reading an item by its index with brackets, so the learner who follows the link reads about a different operation. Property accessors or the Array page fits.

Rated 1, but it is a seven-line program with a stored count, an accumulator and a loop that starts at index 1, so the learner must catch the skipped first item and the bound together. The lesson's other opening items (a plain for...of) are the easy ones; this one is a 2.

The print line uses the in operator ('pc' in kit). No earlier unit and no lesson of this unit introduces in, and the item is not about it; the learner can only learn it from the explanation after answering. Reading the key with kit.pc would test delete without the unknown operator.

The answer is Object.keys(obj), a built-in that no lesson of this track teaches (the lesson teaches for...in and arrays of objects). The hints only say 'a built-in on Object', so the item tests recall of an unseen API rather than the lesson's concept of visiting keys or objects in loops.

Hint 2 says 'a const is not usable until its line', but the snippet declares closing with var, which is exactly the case that is hoisted as undefined. The hint describes a different construct than the one in the code and points the learner toward a ReferenceError instead of the TypeError that is the correct answer.

The lesson concept is losing and fixing this (arrows, bind, call), but this snippet never uses this: bind(null, 3) only presets an argument (partial application). It tests a side feature of bind and not how this is lost or fixed, so it does not exercise the lesson's concept.

The single blank accepts two chips ('water' and '() => water()'), both marked correct. The README rule for FILL_BLANK says each blank is checked on its own and must have exactly one right chip; this item gives the blank two.

The single blank accepts two chips ('lastElementChild' and 'children[2]'), both marked correct. The README rule for FILL_BLANK says each blank is checked on its own and must have exactly one right chip.

In every lesson of this unit the order is predict, concept, trace, fill, parsons, fix. The README says the dom-and-events slots that would be CODE_WRITE become PARSONS or FILL_BLANK, so the intermediate recipe (predict, concept, trace, fill or parsons, fix, then the write slot) puts FIX_BUG fifth and the replacement for the write slot last. Here the replacement item sits before FIX_BUG in all four lessons, and no lesson alternates fill and parsons in the fourth slot.

The second blank accepts both 'appendChild' and 'append', and both chips are marked correct (three correct chips for two blanks). The README rule says each FILL_BLANK blank has exactly one right chip.

This is the first item in the unit to use the event object: the handler reads e.currentTarget.id. No earlier lesson item uses a handler parameter, event-listeners is the only declared prerequisite, and currentTarget is only explained later (fix-01 of this lesson). The learner has to know what currentTarget is to read the output, and neither the prompt nor the hints say it.
The blank accepts two chips ('matches' and 'closest'), both marked correct. The README rule says each FILL_BLANK blank has exactly one right chip.

The snippet builds promises with new Promise and setTimeout, which this unit teaches only in lesson 4 (promise-construction, prerequisite callbacks-and-timers). Lesson 2 declares only promise-chaining and array-map, so the item needs an idea taught later in the unit.

The item tests Function.prototype.call (call, bind and apply chips) for constructor borrowing, not the lesson concept that a class is syntax over prototypes. call/apply/bind is not among the declared prerequisites (constructor-functions, class-inheritance), and the link to classes appears only in the feedback.

Rated 5 (top of the expert track), but 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3 is the best-known floating point gotcha and the fix is a standard tolerance check. It is one of the easiest items of the track, not one of the hardest.

Rated 5, but it is one blank where the standard numeric comparator a - b is chosen from five chips, a pattern taught in the Array methods unit. It is easier than the lesson's fix-01 (rated 4), so the rating does not match the item.

Rated 5, but it is a single blank where the learner picks [...bin] to sort a copy, a pattern from the Array methods and shallow-copy units. It is easier than the lesson's predict-01 and fix-01 and fits 4 at most for the expert track.

Rated 5, but the solution is the standard let-in-a-for-loop closure with the functions called synchronously afterwards (CODE_WRITE cannot run timers). No asynchronous ordering or await is involved and the idea is from the Closures unit, so 5 overstates it.

The snippet is a hand-written binary search (lo, hi, mid, narrowing the range). Binary search is taught in no earlier unit and the item declares only algorithmic-cost and array-reduce, so the learner must already know the algorithm to see why lo = lo + 1 is the bug.

The question is about the single responsibility principle (one reason to change, how to split a class). That is a design-principle topic for the later patterns-and-architecture unit, not behaviour-preserving refactoring, and it is not taught or declared earlier.

The item asks which line to move to separate calculation from printing, a separation-of-concerns design question (its misconceptions are soc-*). It does not test purity or a hidden mutation, and separation of concerns belongs to the later patterns-and-architecture unit.

Rated 5, but it is one blank where the learner reads s.apples + n inside a spread copy; the other chips are obvious mutations or wrong arithmetic. It is among the easiest items of the unit and fits 3 to 4 at most.

Rated 5, but it only asks the learner to pass two functions as arguments (fixedClock, star) instead of calling them. That is first-class function use from the Functions unit, easier than the lesson's concept-01 and no harder than 3 to 4.
